objectives: Secure a negotiated settlement with the UK that allows the Council to approve the measure on schedule in June, avoiding an unresolved Article XXVIII withdrawal threat hanging over the file.
Preserve a meaningful country-specific or otherwise protected share of TRQ access for the UK, sufficient that the UK can present this as real compensation rather than a token gesture.
Avoid the UK joining a coordinated retaliation/dispute front with Japan and Korea over the FTA-disapplication provision.

Protect the EU's broader systemic interest in Article XXVIII credibility — the settlement should not look so generous that Turkey, Korea, India or Japan escalate their own claims expecting similar treatment.
Keep the EU-UK TCA relationship and the parallel UK steel safeguard (where EU exporters hold country allocations) stable — avoid triggering UK retaliation there.
Retain flexibility on the FTA-disapplication clause as a bargaining chip, since it is legally still open and highly sensitive to the UK.
Maintain my own credibility and working relationship with my UK counterpart for future Geneva files, regardless of outcome.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a deal within four rounds giving the UK a country-specific or ring-fenced quota share (or carve-out/product-line protection) plus some review/duration commitment, in exchange for the UK not withdrawing concessions and not joining Japan/Korea in an FTA retaliation front, with Brussels able to close the file by June without member-state revolt. Partial success: no deal, but the UK negotiates bilaterally rather than joining a multilateral bloc, and the eventual UK withdrawal (if any) is narrow and telegraphed rather than a surprise. Failure: talks collapse early, the UK publicly aligns with Japan/Korea against the FTA-disapplication clause, and/or the UK withdraws broad concessions affecting EU exporters under its own safeguard, while other claimants (Turkey, Korea) cite the UK outcome to demand more for themselves.
declaration.approach: Move early and visibly on at least one lower-cost dimension (e.g., signalling openness to a UK-specific quota share, a review clause, or administration method) to create reciprocal movement from the UK, consistent with the belief that momentum pays. Sequence concessions: offer movement on volume/allocation/administration/duration before touching the FTA-disapplication clause, which is the most politically loaded and most linked to the Japan/Korea dispute risk. Use Phase 2 consultations to test Brussels' real flexibility on country shares versus global FCFS, and to flag the Japan/Korea coalition risk as a reason to secure UK settlement even at some cost. Keep language at the table calibrated — avoid committing to specifics that would need to be reopened with Turkey/Korea/India/Japan, since their claims are separate but comparable. Treat the UK's own steel safeguard and TCA linkage as leverage points to explore trade-offs (EU access under UK safeguard for UK access under EU TRQ) rather than concede on FTA-disapplication for free.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A country-specific UK quota share (not global FCFS) reflecting historic trade volumes, protection or carve-out for the narrower range of product lines it is concentrated in, retention of FTA/TCA preferential tariff treatment (resisting disapplication), a review clause, and reciprocal favourable treatment for EU exporters under the UK's own steel safeguard. Politically, the UK needs to show its domestic steel sector a tangible win and will be wary of being seen as accepting less than Turkey or Korea given its concentrated employment impact.

parties.who: Brussels (Council / Trade Policy Committee / Commission mandate holders)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A permanent, defensible legal footing for the steel regime that responds to non-market-economy overcapacity, minimal erosion of the 50%/400,000t global framework, protection of EU steel producers, but also sensitivity from steel-consuming member states wanting continued access. They want the file closed by June without setting a precedent that invites larger asks from Turkey/Korea/India/Japan.

To use the FTA-disapplication clause as leverage, potentially recruiting the UK into a joint dispute or retaliation coalition; they want either removal of the disapplication provision affecting third-country FTA steel trade or compensation of their own, and will watch the UK-EU outcome closely as a benchmark.

parties.who: Turkey and Korea (as principal suppliers with larger volumes)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Larger absolute quota shares given their bigger trade volumes; they will resist any settlement structure that privileges the UK's narrower product concentration over their broader volume-based claim, and may escalate if the UK gets favourable country-specific treatment.
Preservation of market access and possibly a share of the TRQ; less central to this immediate negotiation but watching for precedent.

objectives: Conclude an Article XXVIII settlement with the UK within the four rounds so the Council can vote in June
Preserve a TRQ + high out-of-quota tariff structure that materially reduces tariff-free steel volumes into the EU, especially from non-market-economy sources

Secure a UK-specific quota share (rather than pure global first-come-first-served) that gives the UK enough certainty to settle without setting a precedent other principal suppliers (Turkey, Korea) can point to as excessive generosity
Retain the FTA-disapplication mechanism, or trade it only for something of real value, since it protects the quota from erosion by transshipment/re-origination
Avoid opening the compensation package into unrelated schedule concessions that draw in other member states' sensitivities or invite Council pushback
Get UK movement on its own safeguard's treatment of EU exporters, since EU steel producers face UK country-specific quotas too — this is a two-way file
Keep enough flexibility in duration/review clause to adjust if the regime overshoots or undershoots on import reduction
declaration.success_and_failure: Success is a signed settlement by Round 4 that includes a UK-specific carve-out or share within the TRQ (not just improved global access), a bound out-of-quota rate that still bites (well above zero, even if negotiated down from 50%), a review clause rather than an open-ended commitment, and reciprocal UK movement on EU access under its own safeguard. Failure is either no deal (which blows the June Council vote, invites UK withdrawal of concessions, and hands a win to the 'no compromise' instinct in capitals while doing nothing to actually reduce imports faster) or a deal so generous to the UK that Turkey and Korea demand parity, unravelling the wider regime design and drawing Council/industry criticism that I gave away too much for too little import reduction.
declaration.approach: Move early and visibly on a low-cost, high-signal item — likely duration/review clause or a modest UK-specific sub-quota carved from the global pool — to test whether movement is reciprocated with UK flexibility on the FTA-disapplication point and on EU treatment under the UK's own safeguard. Keep the 50%/400kt headline numbers as anchors rather than opening positions to defend, since walking them back too fast signals weakness to Turkey and Korea who are watching this precedent. Use Phase 2 consultations to test capital appetite before committing anything at the table, and frame every concession internally as conditional and reversible if the UK doesn't reciprocate by Round 2. Prioritise getting a deal that is defensible in the Trade Policy Committee — steel-producing member states need to see real volume reduction; steel-consuming member states need to see the UK is not being scapegoated in a way that provokes a damaging retaliatory spiral over the TCA relationship.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A UK-specific quota share meaningfully larger than what a pure global pool would deliver, protection of the FTA/TCA relationship (i.e. no disapplication of preferential access), a longer transition and a review clause, and reciprocal generous treatment for EU exporters under the UK's own safeguard — because their steel industry is geographically concentrated and politically salient, and a no-deal outcome hurts them more but they know it also blows the EU's June timeline, giving them some leverage.

parties.who: EU member states with steel production (e.g. Germany, Italy, France, Spain)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Maximum import reduction, no generous UK carve-out that undermines the regime's protective effect, and no precedent that Turkey/Korea can exploit.

parties.who: EU member states with steel-consuming manufacturing sectors (e.g. automotive-heavy states)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Enough tariff-free volume and predictable allocation to avoid input cost shocks; wary of an out-of-quota rate that's punitively high with too small a quota.

parties.who: Turkey and Korea (parallel Article XXVIII claims)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Watching this settlement closely as a benchmark; will demand at least equivalent treatment given they ship larger volumes, so I must avoid conceding terms to the UK that are hard to deny them later.
Using threatened retaliation to pressure the EU's overall steel/trade posture, adding urgency to concluding this file quickly and without appearing weak.

objectives: Secure a materially larger UK-specific share of tariff-free access than global first-come-first-served would deliver, ideally a country-specific quota reflecting recent trade volumes with headroom for growth
Prevent or minimise disapplication of TCA/FTA tariff treatment for UK steel exports to the EU
Obtain a workable out-of-quota rate and quota administration mechanism (licensing over pure FCFS) that avoids UK exporters being crowded out early in the year by other suppliers
Secure a review clause and reasonable duration so the measure is not a permanent loss of access

Preserve UK flexibility on its own steel safeguard/Article XXVIII process, avoiding UK concessions to the EU that lock in EU quota shares on UK's own measure beyond what UK's domestic process independently justifies
Avoid a no-deal outcome that triggers UK withdrawal of concessions and mutual escalation, unless capital assesses that is preferable to the EU's opening offer
Preserve working relationship with EU counterpart across the wider Geneva goods agenda
Manage Japan/Korea/Turkey pressure without committing the UK to a joint FTA retaliation that could harden the EU's position or derail a UK-specific settlement
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a UK-specific quota share materially above what pure global FCFS would yield in practice, no disapplication of TCA preferences (or a carve-out/phase-in that neutralises it), a review clause within a bounded duration, and administration that doesn't structurally disadvantage UK exporters — concluded in time for the EU's June Council vote so the UK banks the concession rather than relying on unilateral withdrawal rights. Failure: no deal, EU proceeds with 50%/400kt global FCFS with TCA disapplication and no review, leaving the UK to rely on slow, uncertain, and mutually damaging withdrawal of concessions six months later, while UK steel exporters suffer severe volume loss in the interim with no legal certainty.
declaration.approach: Move early and visibly on process (administration, review clause, enforcement/anti-circumvention, treatment of EU exporters under the UK's own safeguard) where UK flexibility costs little, to test whether the EU reciprocates with movement on the substantive volume/allocation/TCA questions that matter most to UK industry. Signal willingness to engage constructively and quickly given the EU's June deadline — that deadline is leverage for the UK, so avoid rushing to concede it away. Keep the TCA disapplication issue and country-specific share as the two hills to fight on, since these are the biggest determinants of actual UK export volumes. Do not commit to joint action with Japan/Korea/Turkey unless the EU stonewalls, but keep it as a live signal to the EU that non-settlement has costs beyond the UK alone. Report fully and neutrally to London each round, flagging where movement is genuine versus cosmetic, and avoid over-promising a landing zone since no settlement figure has been given.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Conclude quickly enough to hit the June Council vote, minimise compensation elsewhere in the schedule, preserve the 50% bound rate and TRQ structure as the domestic legal backbone, keep flexibility to disapply FTA/TCA preferences to reduce circumvention risk and satisfy protectionist member states, while avoiding a UK withdrawal of concessions or a wider dispute with Turkey/Korea/Japan that complicates the overall steel file.

A tangible, quantifiable improvement in market access certainty for UK steel producers, protection of jobs at concentrated production sites, avoidance of a headline 'no deal' outcome, but also unwilling to trade away the UK's own safeguard leverage over EU exporters cheaply.

Want the UK to join a joint FTA retaliation/dispute to increase pressure on the EU generally on non-market-economy overcapacity measures; their interest is in maximising pressure on the EU's broader steel regime, not specifically in a good UK-EU bilateral outcome, and joint action could serve their interests more than the UK's tailored settlement.

Larger absolute volumes than the UK, so they will push hard on global quota size and may prefer a global FCFS approach over country-specific shares if it preserves their larger relative share; not natural allies for a UK-specific carve-out.
Likely a smaller, more marginal interest, watching precedent-setting on allocation method more than absolute volume.

objectives: Secure a UK-specific country share of the TRQ (not pure global first-come-first-served) sufficient to preserve near-current tariff-free volumes for UK exporters, ideally close to the historic 2.4Mt baseline or a defensible growth trajectory from it

Prevent or limit disapplication of TCA preferences for UK-origin steel; at minimum secure a carve-out or transitional arrangement distinct from other FTA partners given the depth of the UK-EU relationship and parallel safeguard measures
Obtain a review clause and reasonable duration so the regime is not a permanent one-sided ratchet, with mechanisms to revisit volumes/shares as trade patterns evolve
Secure product-line carve-outs or higher sub-quotas for the narrower range of products where UK exports are concentrated, since UK's exposure is concentrated rather than diffuse

Obtain workable quota administration (licensing with predictable access rather than pure first-come-first-served, which structurally disadvantages a mid-sized, concentrated supplier against larger volume shippers like Turkey/Korea)
Preserve negotiating room to trade EU-origin treatment under the UK's own steel safeguard as leverage, without giving away more than necessary

Avoid a settlement so weak that it fails to change the calculus for the two plants at risk of closure, while keeping in reserve the subsidy option and the threat of proportionate withdrawal of concessions
Maintain a credible, defensible narrative for ministers and industry that HMG fought hard and extracted maximum available value, whether or not full settlement is reached
declaration.success_and_failure: Success is a negotiated outcome that secures the UK a country-specific or otherwise ring-fenced share of the TRQ close to historic trade volumes, on administration terms the UK can actually use (not just theoretical access lost to faster-moving competitors), with some duration/review protection and either preserved TCA treatment or an acceptable substitute, achieved without over-conceding on EU access to the UK's own safeguard quota. It is a good outcome if industry and ministers judge it materially better than the EU's original notified terms and better than the no-deal fallback (50% bound rate, 400kt global FCFS, no review). Failure is concluding on terms barely distinguishable from the original notification, or failing to settle and being left only with the slow, costly and uncertain remedy of withdrawing our own concessions six months later, while UK plants close in the interim. A failure is also conceding EU access on our own safeguard for insufficient return, or agreeing a headline volume that looks acceptable but is administered in a way that UK exporters cannot realistically capture (e.g. pure FCFS favouring larger/faster shippers)ough.
declaration.approach: Move early and visibly on at least one dimension we care less about, to test the momentum theory and draw EU movement — likely by signalling flexibility on administration mechanics or duration in exchange for movement on volume/country share, rather than opening with a maximalist blocking position. Anchor hard on the two points that matter most: a UK-specific share (not global pooling) and preservation or graduated phase-out of TCA treatment, since these are the levers that most directly determine whether UK mills stay open. Use the EU's own asymmetric interest — it needs this concluded by June for Council sign-off — as leverage on timing; signal willingness to let this run to round four if the offer is inadequate, since we have a real fallback (withdrawal rights, plus the subsidy option domestically) and the EU's timeline pressure is not matched on our side to the same degree. Keep the UK's own safeguard quota for EU exporters as a deliberately reserved card, only put on the table in later rounds as visible reciprocity for a concrete EU concession on volume or share, not spent early. Coordinate closely with capital between rounds so Geneva's public positioning and capital's private instructions stay aligned, avoiding the appearance of freelancing that could undercut credibility. Frame asks throughout in terms of the shared 'non-market economy overcapacity' rationale the EU itself has invoked — arguing UK steel is a market-economy ally not the intended target — to make a bespoke UK carve-out politically easier for the Commission to defend to its own member states.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A concluded, defensible settlement by June that gives Council-approvable legal cover for the domestic TRQ regime; wants to minimise the number and size of country-specific carve-outs it has to grant (since Turkey and Korea will demand parity), and wants to avoid setting a precedent that undermines the global FCFS model it prefers administratively; will be sensitive to member state split between steel producers (wanting tight quotas) and steel-consuming manufacturers (wanting liberal access), and will look for compensation elsewhere in its schedule that costs it little politically.

parties.who: EU member states via Council/Trade Policy Committee (not at table but shaping Commission mandate)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Steel-producing member states (e.g. potentially aligned with France, Italy, Spain interests) pushing for tight, protective TRQ terms; steel-consuming manufacturing states pushing back for liberal access; overall a Commission mandate that is more protectionist than an idealised free-trade outcome, limiting how far the Geneva seat can move without recourse to capital.

A deal that visibly protects the two at-risk plants and the broader steel workforce; political credit for 'standing up' to the EU; will accept a worse tariff outcome only if paired with either strong compensation elsewhere or a credible parallel subsidy package; will be wary of over-conceding EU access under the UK's own safeguard, since that has its own domestic steel-producer constituency and political sensitivity.

parties.who: UK steel industry and downstream users
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Producers want maximum preserved tariff-free volume and a UK-specific quota with real, capturable access (licensing over pure FCFS); downstream steel-consuming manufacturers in the UK will care more about EU-origin treatment under the UK's own safeguard and may lobby against excessive reciprocal restriction there.

parties.who: Turkey, Korea (larger volume principal suppliers, claims handled separately)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Will seek their own country shares or the largest possible global pool share; any bespoke UK country allocation reduces the residual pool available to them, so the EU will be conscious that generous UK terms invite comparable demands from Turkey and Korea, constraining what the Commission can offer without triggering wider re-negotiation costs.

parties.who: India, Japan (substantial interest, claims handled separately)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Lesser volumes but still want consultation rights respected and no discriminatory disadvantage relative to other suppliers; a background constraint on how differentiated the EU can be in the UK's favour.

public_message: Thank you for joining this first round. The EU opens on the basis set out in our Article XXVIII notification, but we want to signal genuine movement from the outset rather than simply defend the notified text. We propose to raise the global pool from 400,000 to 500,000 tonnes, and — recognising the UK's principal supplying interest and the concentration of UK exports in these specific product lines — to move from pure first-come-first-served to a country-specific allocation, with a UK-specific tranche of 150,000 tonnes. We are also prepared to discuss a reduction in the out-of-quota rate from 50% to 40% as part of a package, a three-year duration with a mandatory review clause, and we are open to discussing how the FTA-disapplication provision interacts specifically with the TCA rather than being treated as a blanket measure. We think this is a serious opening move and we'd like to understand what would allow the UK to reciprocate, including on the treatment of EU exporters under the UK's own safeguard quota.

other_terms: Willingness to discuss bespoke treatment of TCA preferences rather than blanket FTA disapplication
Expectation of reciprocal discussion on EU exporters' allocations under the UK's own steel safeguard
Openness to circumvention/enforcement provisions to be negotiated jointly

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A substantive counter on tranche size and out-of-quota rate, rather than a rejection of the country-specific approach
expectations.why: We have moved first on volume, allocation method and rate; reciprocity should follow if the UK values momentum as much as we do

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Support for testing this opening without yet locking in final figures
expectations.why: This is a first move designed to draw a UK counter and test their floor, not a final offer; capitals need room to adjust in later rounds

private_rationale: Opening with visible movement (pool up, country-specific tranche, rate down, review clause, TCA flexibility signalled) is consistent with the belief that early movement draws reciprocal movement, and it gives us a defensible narrative in Geneva that we are negotiating in good faith - useful both for the UK relationship and for optics with Japan/Korea/Turkey/India watching this process, reducing the incentive for a joint UK-Japan-Korea retaliation coalition. But the offer still keeps the out-of-quota rate well above zero, keeps duration short with review (so Brussels/Council retain future leverage and member states with steel-producing interests are not locked into a permanent giveaway), and does not yet concede on FTA disapplication beyond agreeing to discuss the TCA specifically. This leaves room to move further in rounds 2-4 while testing whether the UK reciprocates on the EU-exporter treatment under the UK's own safeguard, which is a key EU ask not yet addressed by the UK side ownership of the parallel process.

public_message: We welcome the movement, and we recognise the political difficulty of moving off the notified text this quickly. But let's be candid about scale: 150,000 tonnes against a three-year average of 2.4 million tonnes is a reduction of over 90% in tariff-free access on lines where the UK is a principal supplying interest. That is not compensation, it is the injury itself. We need a country-specific tranche that reflects historical trade shares, not a token allocation dressed as one. Our opening position: a total pool of 1.5 million tonnes, with a UK-specific tranche of 900,000 tonnes, an out-of-quota rate no higher than 15%, and a two-year duration with a mandatory, data-triggered review rather than a discretionary one. On the FTA-disapplication point, we want UK-origin steel treated on TCA terms in full — not carved out into a separate discussion later, but settled here as part of this package, given the TCA already contains its own safeguard architecture that makes a blanket disapplication both unnecessary and disproportionate. On your question about our own safeguard: we are willing to look seriously at the treatment of EU exporters under the UK measure, including their country-specific allocation, as part of a reciprocal package — but we need to see the shape of the EU's real landing zone on volume and rate before we can put specifics on that table. We're moving in good faith. We'd like to see the next move address tranche size directly rather than duration or review mechanics, which are secondary to us.

report: First round produced real movement from both sides but a wide gap remains. We opened with 500,000t global pool, a 150,000t UK-specific tranche, 40% out-of-quota rate, 3-year duration with mandatory review, and floated TCA-specific treatment of the FTA-disapplication provision rather than a blanket rule. UK's counter: 1.5m tonne pool, 900,000t UK tranche, out-of-quota rate capped at 15%, 2-year duration with a data-triggered mandatory review, and full TCA-terms treatment for UK-origin steel settled now rather than deferred. UK explicitly deprioritised duration/review mechanics and asked us to move on tranche size next. UK also signalled conditional willingness to discuss EU exporters' treatment under their own safeguard quota, but only once they see our 'real landing zone' on volume/rate — this is a card they are deliberately holding back. No agreement possible this round; both sides are still in opening-to-second-move territory. No hostile signals on the Japan/Korea angle, but the UK's insistence on TCA-full-terms treatment intersects directly with that risk — satisfying UK on this point cheaply would help detach them from any Korea/Japan-driven joint retaliation strategy against FTA disapplication generally.

recommendation.reasoning: We should keep momentum by moving again, but not close the gap in one step — the UK's 900,000t ask is far beyond what Council can sell to producer member states, and matching UK on out-of-quota rate this early removes leverage for later rounds. A move to a ~650,000t pool with a ~250,000t UK tranche and a rate cut to 35% shows continued good faith without capitulating on scale. Duration and review are low-cost to us since the UK itself flagged them as secondary — we can hold our 3-year/mandatory-review position as a stable anchor while spending movement on tranche and rate, which the UK says it actually cares about. Separately, offering to settle the FTA-disapplication issue specifically on TCA terms is cheap for us relative to the risk of a UK-Japan-Korea joint FTA retaliation strategy, and should be used deliberately to peel the UK away from that coalition dynamic.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Mandate flexibility to move the global pool toward 600,000-700,000 tonnes and the UK-specific tranche toward 250,000-300,000 tonnes in Round 2, with confirmation of Council/member state tolerance for a further reduction in the out-of-quota rate toward 30-35%.
requests.why: The UK has signalled tranche size and rate are their real priorities, and has deprioritised duration/review. Meeting them partway on their stated priority preserves momentum without exhausting our negotiating room, and tests whether they will reciprocate on the safeguard treatment they are currently withholding.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Authority to offer explicit TCA-specific treatment of the FTA-disapplication clause (rather than blanket disapplication) as a firm element of any final package.
requests.why: This is a comparatively low-cost concession for us and directly addresses the UK's stated red line. It also reduces the risk of the UK joining a Japan/Korea-led joint FTA dispute over disapplication, which would be more damaging to our broader Geneva position than a targeted TCA carve-out.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Guidance on how much weight to give the UK's conditional offer on EU exporters' treatment under their own safeguard measure before we make further concessions on volume/rate.
requests.why: The UK is holding this back deliberately as leverage. We should decide now whether to press for specifics on this in Round 2 as a condition of further EU movement, or continue moving unilaterally to sustain the momentum strategy Brussels has approved.

private_rationale: The UK's opening ask (900k tranche, 15% rate, full TCA treatment, 2-year term) is a strong opening bid designed to test our resolve — it is far outside what Council will approve given producer-state sensitivities, but the gap is not necessarily unbridgeable given both sides moved in round one. My real concern is the Japan/Korea coalition risk: if the UK feels cornered on the FTA-disapplication point, they have an incentive to bloc with Korea/Japan and disapply TCA provisions in a way that would be much costlier to unwind than a bespoke TCA carve-out here. I want to spend concessions cheaply on that specific issue while holding firm on aggregate volume, using the momentum principle to keep UK engaged without revealing our real floor (likely somewhere near 300-350k tonnes tranche, 30% out-of-quota, 3-year term) too early. I also want Brussels to press the UK on reciprocity regarding EU exporters under their safeguard — we should not let the UK bank concessions here while keeping their own measure's treatment of us vague indefinitely.

instruction: Move to Round 2 with a calibrated second offer, not a capitulation. Table: global pool of 600,000 tonnes, UK-specific tranche of 250,000 tonnes, country-specific allocation, out-of-quota rate reduced from 40% to 35%, duration held at 3 years with a mandatory review clause — but reframe the review as data-triggered (linked to import volume/price thresholds) to meet the UK's stated preference on mechanics without giving up the anchor of a 3-year term. On FTA disapplication: offer explicit TCA-specific treatment (UK-origin steel treated under TCA rules rather than blanket disapplication) as a firm element of the landing zone — but make this conditional, explicitly, on the UK now putting concrete detail on the table regarding treatment of EU exporters under the UK's own safeguard quota. Do not let this be open-ended reciprocity — say clearly that further EU movement on tranche size or rate in Round 3 depends on seeing the shape of the UK offer on EU exporters' country allocation. We are not matching their 900,000t ask or their 15% rate; hold firm that these are outside what Council can sell, and say so plainly rather than leaving it implicit. If they push back on scale, remind them that a no-deal outcome reverts to the notified 400,000t/50%/global FCFS text, which is worse for them than continued negotiation, and that time pressure cuts both ways given the June Council deadline. Keep tone collaborative — we still want this landed by June — but the free unilateral movement phase ends here; the next EU move must be matched by a substantive UK move on their own safeguard treatment of EU exporters.

authority.notes: Ceilings for Round 2: offer 600,000t pool / 250,000t UK tranche / 35% out-of-quota rate as the actual table position; 700,000t/300,000t/30% are absolute Round 2 limits not to be disclosed. Duration to remain 3 years but review clause should be recast as data-triggered rather than purely discretionary to address UK's stated mechanics preference at no real cost. TCA-specific treatment of the FTA-disapplication clause is authorised as a firm offer, but must be explicitly conditioned on the UK providing concrete detail on EU exporters' treatment under the UK's own safeguard quota before Round 3. Do not move further on volume or rate without that reciprocal detail on the table.

response_to_requests.request: Mandate flexibility to move pool toward 600-700k and UK tranche toward 250-300k, with rate toward 30-35%
response_to_requests.why: This matches the UK's stated priorities (tranche/rate over duration/review) and sustains momentum, but ceilings are set so Round 2 doesn't exhaust our room before we've tested UK reciprocity.

response_to_requests.request: Authority to offer TCA-specific treatment of FTA-disapplication as a firm package element
response_to_requests.why: Low-cost for us, addresses UK's stated concern, and reduces risk of UK aligning with Japan/Korea on a joint FTA disapplication challenge — but tie it explicitly to reciprocity so it isn't given away for free.

response_to_requests.request: Guidance on weight to give UK's conditional offer on EU exporters' treatment under their safeguard
response_to_requests.why: Do not continue moving unilaterally. Treat this as the price of further EU movement: press for specifics now, and make clear no further tranche/rate concessions come until the UK shows its hand on this. This converts their leverage point into ours.

private_rationale: The UK has told us plainly what it values (tranche size, rate) and what it will trade (deferred, conditional detail on its own safeguard treatment of EU exporters). If we keep moving unilaterally on volume/rate without extracting that detail, we lose our best point of leverage — the UK's own measure directly harms EU exporters and is the one lever the UK cares about protecting from scrutiny. Round 2 should look generous on the surface (raising pool, tranche, cutting rate, offering TCA carve-out) while quietly converting the momentum strategy into a hinge: further EU concessions are now contingent on UK reciprocity on its own measure. This preserves Council-sellability (we are not yet near their 900k ask, we're not near their 15% rate) while testing whether the UK's good-faith signals translate into real reciprocal movement. report:
The EU opened with a modest improvement on its notified position: global pool raised from 400,000 to 500,000 tonnes, a shift from FCFS to country-specific allocation with a UK tranche of 150,000 tonnes, a possible reduction in the out-of-quota rate from 50% to 40%, a three-year duration with a mandatory review clause, and openness to narrowing the FTA-disapplication provision so it interacts with the TCA rather than blanket-disapplying it. They explicitly invited a reciprocal move on treatment of EU exporters under our own safeguard quota.

I pushed back hard on scale: a 150,000t UK tranche against our 2.4m tonne three-year average is a >90% cut in tariff-free access and amounts to the injury itself, not compensation. I tabled an opening UK position of a 1.5m tonne total pool, 900,000t UK-specific tranche, out-of-quota rate capped at 15%, two-year duration with a mandatory data-triggered review, and full TCA treatment for UK-origin steel rather than a deferred carve-out discussion. I signalled willingness to discuss EU exporter treatment under our own safeguard reciprocally, but made clear we need to see their real landing zone on volume/rate first. I flagged that we want the next EU move to address tranche size directly, not duration/review mechanics.

Read of the room: the EU's move to country-specific allocation and openness to narrowing the FTA/TCA interaction are the two most useful signals — they suggest the June deadline is generating real pressure. But the volume gap (150k vs 900k) is still enormous and is the crux. Rate (40% vs 15%) is secondary but will matter for the final package value. They did not push back on our TCA framing, which I read as a soft acceptance that the disapplication provision is negotiable in substance, not just presentationally.

recommendation.reasoning: No agreement is possible yet — the gap between 150,000 and 900,000 tonnes is too wide to settle in round one, and settling prematurely at the EU's current tranche would leave UK exporters facing a near-90% loss of tariff-free access, which I understand to be politically and industrially unacceptable. The EU has shown genuine (if small) movement on allocation method and the TCA interaction, which is worth banking rhetorically but not worth trading away leverage for yet. I recommend continuing to press on tranche size specifically, since the EU itself asked us to focus there, and holding rate/duration/review as secondary levers to concede in exchange for tranche movement. I am not recommending a settlement figure to capital at this stage — I need instructions on the UK's actual floor for the tranche and how much weight to give the safeguard-reciprocity linkage before I can responsibly recommend acceptance of any package in round 2 or 3.
